turns.text: It helps your brain start adjusting before you land.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I watched a horror film last night and had nightmares all night. I'm thirty four. This is embarrassing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not embarrassing at all. Scary films right before bed keep your brain on alert, at any age.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm supposed to watch the sequel with my friends tonight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then watch something light afterwards, even twenty minutes of a comedy, to reset your mood before bed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually / a really good plan.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And leave a small lamp on if it helps. No shame.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe I'll bring a comedy for everyone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Your friends might secretly thank you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My lower back aches when I wake up. Could it be how I'm sleeping?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Quite possibly. Do you sleep on your back, side, or stomach?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Stomach, mostly. Face squished into the pillow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stomach sleeping can arch your lower back. Try putting a flat pillow under your hips, or slowly training yourself onto your side.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Side with / a pillow between my knees?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly that. It keeps your hips level and takes pressure off your back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if my mattress is just old?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If it sags in the middle or it's over eight years old, it could be part of the problem too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm retired and I wake up at five every morning, wide awake. Drives my wife mad.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very common as we get older, our body clocks tend to shift earlier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I change it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Somewhat. Getting bright light in the late afternoon and evening, like a walk at five, can nudge your clock later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And in the morning? I tend to / make tea and wander around.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep the lights low and stay quiet so you don't wake her. Some early risers enjoy that hour for reading.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do love the quiet, honestly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then maybe it's not a problem, just a different rhythm.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hotel room tonight, right next to the lift. I can hear it every time it dings.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask the front desk if they can move you. It's a very common request, and they often have quieter rooms.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I asked. They're full.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then earplugs if you have them, or play white noise on your phone. A fan noise works well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No earplugs. But I've got / my headphones.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Soft foam headphones with rain sounds can block a lot. Also roll a towel along the bottom of the door, it cuts hallway noise.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A towel. Never would have thought of that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Old hotel trick. Hope you get some rest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can only fit in my workouts at ten at night. Is that wrecking my sleep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For some people it does, because intense exercise raises your heart rate and body temperature. Others sleep fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know which one I am?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Notice how long it takes to fall asleep on workout nights versus rest nights.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hmm. Now that you say it, / workout nights I'm up till one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try to finish at least ninety minutes before bed, or do lighter stuff late, like stretching or yoga.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I could lift weights in the morning on weekends.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a nice mix. Your body will thank you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My husband snoozes his alarm five times. I wake up at every single one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's maddening. Could he set one alarm for the real time and put his phone across the room?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He says he needs the snoozes to wake up gently.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A sunrise light or a gradual volume alarm gives him gentle without five alarms.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll pitch that. Will he / go for it though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe frame it as a gift. A gadget feels less like a complaint.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, very diplomatic.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And earplugs for you until it arrives.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I catch up on sleep at the weekend? I do five hours on weeknights.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little, but not fully. Weekend lie-ins help, but your body still feels the deficit during the week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So it's pointless?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not pointless, but sleeping in until noon can shift your body clock, and Monday morning hurts more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Monday is / always brutal, yeah.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try to get even thirty more minutes on weeknights, and keep weekend lie-ins to an hour or so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thirty minutes I can probably manage.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small changes like that add up fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My dorm roommate studies till three with the big light on. I'm losing it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's tough. Have you talked to her about it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sort of. I hinted.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try being direct but friendly. Ask if she could use a desk lamp after midnight instead of the main light.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She'd probably say yes / if I actually asked.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most people do. Meanwhile, a good eye mask can save your nights.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll talk to her tonight. Wish me luck.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You've got this. Offer to chip in for the lamp if it helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I get up to pee three times a night. It's ruining my sleep.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try to drink most of your water earlier in the day, and slow down in the last two hours before bed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do drink a huge glass right before bed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's probably part of it. Tea and alcohol in the evening can also make it worse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I cut back / and it still happens?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's worth checking with a doctor. Frequent waking to pee can have medical causes, and they're often easy to treat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll try the water thing first.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give it a couple of weeks and see.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is reading on an e-reader as bad as scrolling my phone?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually much better. E-readers with e-ink screens don't glow like phones, and there are no notifications pulling you in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine has a backlight though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most have a warm light setting, turn that on and keep the brightness low.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So / it's fine then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pretty much. The main thing is that a book doesn't keep you hooked the way social media does, unless it's a thriller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It is a thriller.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then maybe stop at the end of a chapter, not the middle of a cliffhanger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Big job interview tomorrow and I'm already lying in bed wired.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally normal. Even if you don't sleep perfectly, one rough night won't ruin your interview. Adrenaline will carry you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually comforting.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good. Try not to check the time, it just adds pressure. Turn the clock away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My outfit's ready, I've / practised my answers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you're prepared. Tell yourself that, and let your mind wander to something boring, like naming fruits from A to Z.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Apple, banana, cherry.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it. Take your time with each one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My cat wakes me up at five every day screaming for breakfast.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: She's trained you well. Cats learn quickly that yowling gets food.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So how do I untrain / her?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Don't feed her straight after the yowling, even if it's hard. Wait until your usual time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She'll scream louder.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For a few days, yes. An automatic feeder set for five can also help, she starts waiting for the machine instead of you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ooh. Then I'm not the food god anymore.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. The machine gets the blame.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Summer holidays are ending and my kids have been going to bed at eleven. School starts in a week.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A week is enough if you start now. Bring bedtime earlier by about twenty minutes every night or two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And mornings? They've been sleeping till ten.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Same idea, wake them a bit earlier each day too. Mornings actually matter even more for shifting their body clocks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They'll / grumble, no doubt about it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably. Make mornings more appealing, breakfast in the garden or something fun planned, and keep evenings calm with dimmer lights.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Pancakes might work. They'd get up at dawn for pancakes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pancakes are a powerful motivator. Use them wisely.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I work from bed most days. My laptop basically lives there. Is that bad for sleep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can. Your brain starts linking the bed with work and alertness, which makes switching off harder.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My flat's tiny though. There's / no desk.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even a small corner works. A chair and a fold-down table at the kitchen counter is enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Really? Just that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's about having a different spot. At night, the bed becomes just for sleep again.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll try the kitchen counter tomorrow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pack the laptop away when you finish, too. Out of sight helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ate a massive curry at ten and now I've got heartburn lying down.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ouch. Prop yourself up with an extra pillow so your head and chest are higher. Lying on your left side can also help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Left side. Okay, that's / slightly better.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sip some water, and avoid lying totally flat for a bit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I eat earlier in future?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you can, finish big meals at least two or three hours before bed. Spicy and fatty food late is a classic trigger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Lesson learned. Worth it though, it was a great curry.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds like it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I really need eight hours of sleep? I feel fine on six.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most adults need about seven to nine, but there's some variation. A few people genuinely do well on less.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How would I know?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Do you need an alarm to wake up? Do you crash in the afternoon, or doze off in meetings?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, all three. / Yes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you might be running on a sleep debt you've got used to. Try seven hours for two weeks and see how you feel.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Seven. That's a whole extra hour of my evening gone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe, but you might get more done in the hours you're awake.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We moved into an old house last week and I can't sleep. Every creak sounds like someone on the stairs.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's really normal in a new place. Your brain stays a little on guard until the noises become familiar.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long does that last?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually a week or two. It helps to learn the sounds, the pipes cooling, the floorboards settling, the boiler clicking on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The boiler. That's probably / the thumping at midnight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very likely. A quiet fan or white noise can cover the random sounds while you adjust.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And maybe I'll check the locks before bed so I stop wondering.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good idea. A little routine like that tells your mind the house is safe.

option_sets.lead_in: I've been sleeping badly, and I want to try something new. Can you help me pick?
options: The first idea is going to bed at exactly the same time every night, even on weekends.
Then there's no screens for an hour before bed and reading a paper book instead.
Option three is buying a white noise machine because my street is pretty loud at night.
And the last one is cutting out coffee after lunch, which would be really hard for me.
moshi_comment: Since your street is loud, the white noise machine might give you the quickest improvement. A steady bedtime is one of the most reliable habits for better sleep in general. Cutting afternoon coffee is tough, but it can make a real difference.
What usually keeps you up, is it noise, a busy mind, or just not feeling tired? If it's noise, try the white noise machine first. If you're not tired, cutting afternoon coffee is worth a shot.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm buying a new mattress and I've narrowed it down.
options: One is a firm memory foam mattress that a lot of reviews say is great for back pain.
Another is a soft pillow top spring mattress, really cozy, but it might sag after a few years.
Or there's a hybrid with springs and foam, medium firm, and a bit more expensive.
moshi_comment: The hybrid is often a good balance of support and comfort, and medium firm suits most sleepers. The firm foam one is worth a look if your back hurts. The pillow top feels lovely in the store but may not last as long.
Do you sleep on your side, back or stomach? Side sleepers usually like something softer, so the hybrid could be ideal. If you have back pain, I'd try the firm foam one.

option_sets.lead_in: My neck hurts every morning, so I'm shopping for a new pillow.
options: There's a contoured memory foam pillow with a dip in the middle for your head.
Or a classic feather pillow, soft and squishy, that you can punch into shape.
A buckwheat pillow full of little husks, which apparently stays cool and supports well but rustles.
moshi_comment: For neck pain, the contoured foam is often the most supportive. Feathers are comfy but flatten during the night, and buckwheat is a great middle ground if the rustling doesn't bother you.
If you sleep on your side, the contoured one or buckwheat will hold your neck better. The feather pillow is lovely to sink into, but it's the least likely to fix the ache.

option_sets.lead_in: My dog has started sleeping in our bed and I need to decide what to do about it.
options: We could buy him a nice dog bed and put it right next to ours, so he's still close.
Or crate train him in the kitchen at night with a blanket over the crate.
We could just give up and let him stay in the bed, he's a small dog after all.
Or close the bedroom door and let him have the whole living room sofa.
moshi_comment: A dog bed beside yours is usually the gentlest change, he stays near you without kicking you at night. The crate works well too but takes more training, while letting him stay or giving him the sofa depends on how much you mind the fur.

If you're sleeping badly, the bed beside yours is the best compromise. The crate is good if he's anxious and likes a den, the sofa is easy but could become a habit, and keeping him in your bed is only fine if you both sleep well.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to track my sleep for a month, and I'm not sure which way to do it.
options: Wear a fitness watch to bed, which tracks heart rate and when I wake up.
Use a free app that sits on the mattress and listens for movement and snoring.
Or just keep a paper diary on my nightstand, writing bedtime and how rested I feel.
moshi_comment: The watch gives you the most data without effort, but some people find it uncomfortable at night. The app is free and catches snoring, while the paper diary is surprisingly useful because it records how you actually feel.
A simple diary plus the free app is a great combination for a month. The watch is nice if you already own one, but don't worry too much about its exact sleep stages.

option_sets.lead_in: My bedroom is way too bright in summer and I'm figuring out how to make it darker.
options: Thick blackout curtains that cover the whole window and a bit past the edges.
A comfy silk eye mask, which is cheap but I always pull it off in my sleep.
Fitted blackout blinds inside the window frame, a bit pricey and need installing.
Or temporary blackout film stuck on the glass, which looks a bit strange from the street.
moshi_comment: Fitted blinds give the darkest room, especially with curtains layered on top. Blackout curtains alone are a solid choice, the eye mask is fine for travel, and the film is a quick fix if you rent.
Since you pull masks off, the curtains or the fitted blinds will suit you better. The film is the cheapest way to go dark, it just looks odd from outside.
